subtopic_detail: A flat red facial birthmark occupying the forehead and upper eyelid in a well six week old infant
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a six week old boy referred by his general practitioner because of a birthmark that has been present since birth. His mother says it has not grown or thickened, but it deepens in colour when he cries.

He is breastfeeding well and his weight is tracking along the 50th centile. He has had no seizures or unusual movements, and he smiles responsively at his mother.

data_table.Examination: Flat pink to red patch covering the right forehead, the right upper eyelid and the skin over the right cheekbone, sharply demarcated at the midline, partially blanching with pressure, with no thickening, nodularity or ulceration; red reflexes present and symmetrical, corneal diameters appear equal, fixes and follows past the midline, anterior fontanelle soft, tone and limb movements symmetrical, head circumference on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Refer him for pulsed dye laser therapy and review the appearance of the skin at twelve months
options.rationale: Pulsed dye laser is the treatment of choice for the skin lesion itself and early treatment does improve colour, but arranging it as the sole action leaves the neurological and ocular associations of a lesion in this distribution unsearched. Laser referral belongs alongside, not instead of, imaging and ophthalmology review. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Capillary malformation)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Capillary malformation

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and refer him for an ophthalmology assessment
options.rationale: A capillary malformation involving the forehead and upper eyelid carries a substantial risk of leptomeningeal vascular malformation and of ipsilateral glaucoma, so brain imaging and formal ophthalmological assessment are both indicated even when the infant is neurologically well. Glaucoma may be present at birth or develop later, which is why ophthalmology review is arranged now and then repeated. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Capillary malformation)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Capillary malformation
BMJ Best Practice: Sturge-Weber syndrome

options.text: Reassure the parents that the patch will fade over months and review him at his next immunisation visit
options.rationale: Fading is the natural history of a salmon patch on the glabella or nape, not of a capillary malformation, which persists and darkens with age. Reassurance without imaging or eye review would miss both intracranial involvement and a glaucoma that can threaten vision in the first year. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Kids Health Info on birthmarks)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Kids Health Info on birthmarks

options.text: Commence oral propranolol after a baseline electrocardiogram and paediatric cardiology review
options.rationale: Propranolol is the treatment for a proliferating infantile haemangioma, which is a vascular tumour that appears after birth, grows for several months and feels raised and firm. A lesion that has been flat and unchanged since birth is a malformation and does not respond to propranolol. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Kids Health Info on birthmarks)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Kids Health Info on birthmarks

options.text: Arrange cranial ultrasound through the anterior fontanelle now and repeat the scan at six months of age
options.rationale: Cranial ultrasound images the ventricles and midline structures but does not show the cortical and leptomeningeal changes that matter here, and a normal scan would give false reassurance. Magnetic resonance imaging is the study that answers the question being asked. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Sturge-Weber syndrome)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Sturge-Weber syndrome

explanation.summary: A capillary malformation, still widely called a port wine stain, is present at birth, grows with the child and does not involute. Its importance lies in its distribution: involvement of the forehead and upper eyelid, which follows the developmental territory supplied by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, is the pattern associated with leptomeningeal angiomatosis and with ipsilateral glaucoma. Children with intracranial involvement present with focal seizures, hemiparesis and developmental regression, most often in the first two years, and early recognition allows seizure treatment and developmental support to be arranged before damage accumulates. Glaucoma occurs in up to a third of children with upper eyelid involvement and can present at any age, so ophthalmology follow up is ongoing rather than a single visit. Pulsed dye laser remains the treatment for the skin itself and is most effective when started early.
key_points: A capillary malformation is flat at birth, persists lifelong and darkens with age, unlike an infantile haemangioma which appears after birth and proliferates.
Forehead and upper eyelid involvement is the distribution linked to leptomeningeal vascular malformation and to ipsilateral glaucoma.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging and formal ophthalmology assessment are both arranged even when the infant is neurologically normal.
Cranial ultrasound cannot exclude leptomeningeal involvement and a normal scan is falsely reassuring.
Pulsed dye laser treats the cutaneous lesion and is complementary to, not a substitute for, the associated screening.
explanation.pearls: Eyelid involvement is the ocular red flag: children with upper eyelid capillary malformation need intraocular pressure measured at diagnosis and then at least annually through childhood, because glaucoma in this group frequently develops after the first year rather than at birth.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Capillary malformation
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Kids Health Info on birthmarks

subtopic_detail: Recurrent bilateral evening leg pain in a thriving six year old with a normal examination and normal daytime function
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a six year old boy whose mother is worried about leg pains. For about four months he has woken crying two or three evenings a week, pointing to both calves and the fronts of both thighs, and settles after twenty minutes of rubbing and cuddles.

He is fully himself the next morning, walks to school and plays soccer on Saturdays without complaint. His weight and height are tracking along the 50th centile and he has had no fevers, weight loss or rashes.

data_table.Examination: Gait normal with normal heel toe pattern and normal running, no limp, no joint swelling, warmth or effusion, full and painless range of movement at hips, knees and ankles, no bony tenderness on direct palpation of the tibiae or femora, no muscle wasting, spine straight with normal forward flexion, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no bruising or petechiae

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Explain the benign pattern to the family, advise massage and simple analgesia, and review if the pattern changes
options.rationale: Bilateral limb pain confined to evenings and nights, with a child who is completely well and fully active by day and who has a normal examination, is the recognised benign idiopathic pattern and needs no investigation. Safety netting matters because the diagnosis is defined by its natural history: unilateral pain, daytime pain, limp, joint swelling or systemic features change the assessment. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on limb pain in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on limb pain in children

options.text: Order a full blood count with blood film and inflammatory markers, and review him when the results return
options.rationale: Blood tests are the right move when pain is unilateral, persistent through the day, associated with a limp, or accompanied by pallor, bruising, lymphadenopathy or organomegaly, none of which are present here. Investigating a classical benign pattern generates false positive results and entrenches the family's anxiety. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on limb pain in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on limb pain in children

options.text: Request plain radiographs of both tibiae and femora, and arrange orthopaedic review of the films with the family
options.rationale: Radiographs are indicated for focal bony tenderness, night pain in one limb, or a limp, because those features raise osteoid osteoma, osteomyelitis and bone tumour. Symmetrical pain with no bony tenderness does not warrant irradiating both lower limbs. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on limb pain in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on limb pain in children

options.text: Refer him to a paediatric rheumatologist for assessment of possible juvenile idiopathic arthritis and its treatment
options.rationale: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis produces joint swelling with morning stiffness that eases through the day, which is the reverse of this boy's pattern of an entirely normal morning and evening pain. A normal joint examination with no morning stiffness makes the referral unnecessary. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology

options.text: Check serum vitamin D and calcium levels, and commence a cholecalciferol supplement while awaiting the results
options.rationale: Vitamin D deficiency causes bone pain with tenderness over the long bones, proximal weakness and sometimes deformity, and is tested when there are risk factors such as limited sun exposure or a restrictive diet. Neither the history nor the examination here points that way. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vitamin D deficiency)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vitamin D deficiency

explanation.summary: Benign idiopathic limb pain of childhood affects up to a third of primary school aged children and is defined by a highly consistent pattern rather than by exclusion through investigation. The pain is bilateral, affects the muscles of the calves, shins and thighs rather than the joints, occurs in the late afternoon, evening or night, and resolves completely by morning with no residual limp or functional loss. The examination is normal, growth is unaffected, and the child is not systemically unwell. The differentials that genuinely demand investigation announce themselves through asymmetry, persistence into the day, or systemic features, so the clinical task is pattern recognition plus explicit safety netting rather than a screening panel of tests. Families are helped by being told that the pain is real, that it is not caused by growth of the bones, and that it settles over months to years.
key_points: The benign pattern is bilateral, muscular rather than articular, confined to evening and night, and fully resolved by the next morning.
A normal gait, normal joints and absence of bony tenderness are the findings that support the diagnosis positively.
Unilateral pain, daytime pain, limp, joint swelling, fever, weight loss, pallor or bruising redirect the assessment towards malignancy, infection and inflammatory arthritis.
Investigations are not required when the pattern is classical, and incidental abnormal results cause harm.
Explicit safety netting substitutes for testing and should name the features that would prompt earlier review.
explanation.pearls: Leukaemia presenting as limb pain typically produces pain that persists into the day and is accompanied by a cytopenia in at least one lineage, so a child who runs and plays normally every morning and has a normal blood count taken for other reasons is very unlikely to have it.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on limb pain in children
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vitamin D deficiency

subtopic_detail: Refusal to weight bear after a witnessed twisting fall in a toddler whose initial radiographs are reported as normal
stem:
You are the emergency department resident assessing an 18 month old girl who will not walk. Yesterday afternoon her father watched her catch her foot at the bottom of a slide at the park and twist as she came off it, and she cried immediately and has not borne weight since.

She crawls, plays and feeds normally and settles with paracetamol. Her father is with her and gives a consistent account, and her growth and developmental milestones are age appropriate.

data_table.Examination: Refuses to stand on the right leg but moves it spontaneously when lying, tenderness on palpation over the lower third of the right tibia, no deformity, no swelling, no bruising anywhere on the body, hips and knees with full painless range of movement, no warmth over any joint, skin and frenulum intact
data_table.Investigations: Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the right tibia and fibula reported as showing no fracture, C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange an urgent technetium bone scan today and admit her under the orthopaedic team pending the result
options.rationale: A bone scan will show increased uptake but exposes a toddler to radiation and to the need for sedation in order to answer a question that immobilisation and a repeat radiograph answer safely. It is reserved for persisting unexplained refusal to weight bear after simpler steps. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child

options.text: Discharge her with simple analgesia and advise her father to return only if she is still not walking in one week
options.rationale: Discharge without immobilisation leaves an undisplaced spiral fracture unsupported and prolongs pain, and a week of walking on it risks displacement. Analgesia is necessary but is not on its own an adequate plan for a child with focal bony tenderness. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child

options.text: Immobilise the leg in a below knee cast, provide analgesia, and review her with repeat radiographs in ten days
options.rationale: An undisplaced spiral fracture of the tibial shaft in a newly walking child is frequently invisible on the initial films and becomes apparent as periosteal reaction on a film repeated a week to ten days later. Treating on clinical grounds with immobilisation gives symptom relief and protects the bone while the diagnosis declares itself. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child

options.text: Request an ultrasound of both hips looking for an effusion and aspirate the joint if any fluid is demonstrated
options.rationale: Hip ultrasound is the right test when the pain localises to the hip or groin, when the hip is held flexed and externally rotated, or when there is fever with raised inflammatory markers. Tenderness over the tibial shaft with pain free hip movement and a normal C reactive protein points elsewhere. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child

options.text: Admit her for a skeletal survey and fundoscopy, and notify the state child protection service before discharge
options.rationale: A skeletal survey is indicated when the injury does not fit the developmental stage or the stated mechanism, when there are multiple or unexplained bruises, or when the account changes, none of which apply to a witnessed twisting injury in an independently mobile toddler with an intact skin examination. A spiral tibial fracture in this age group is a common accidental injury and is not in itself suspicious. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on child abuse)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on child abuse

explanation.summary: The toddler fracture is an undisplaced spiral or oblique fracture of the distal tibial shaft that follows a low energy twisting injury in a child between about nine months and three years, and around half are not visible on the first radiographs. The diagnosis is therefore clinical, resting on refusal to weight bear with focal tibial tenderness after a mechanism that involves rotation. Management is immobilisation for comfort and protection, with a repeat radiograph after seven to ten days showing periosteal new bone if the fracture was present. The important alternatives are septic arthritis and osteomyelitis, which bring fever and raised inflammatory markers, transient synovitis, which localises to the hip, and inflicted injury, which is suggested by a mechanism that does not match the child's developmental abilities. Healing is rapid and the great majority need nothing beyond a cast or boot for three to four weeks.
key_points: Around half of toddler fractures are radiographically occult at presentation, so a normal first film does not exclude one.
Focal tenderness over the tibial shaft with refusal to weight bear after a twisting mechanism is enough to treat.
Immobilisation plus a repeat radiograph at seven to ten days is the standard pathway and avoids irradiating or sedating the child further.
Fever with raised inflammatory markers or a hip held flexed and externally rotated redirects to infection or synovitis.
Inflicted injury is suggested by a mechanism inconsistent with the child's mobility, changing accounts, or associated bruising, not by the fracture pattern alone.
explanation.pearls: Periosteal new bone becomes visible on plain film from about seven to ten days after a toddler fracture, which is why the review radiograph is booked for that window rather than at three or four days when it will still look normal.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on the limping child
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on child abuse
BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of limp in children

subtopic_detail: Vulval soreness with intermittent non bloody discharge in a five year old girl with normal external genital examination
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a five year old girl brought by her mother with six weeks of vulval soreness and itch. Her mother has noticed a pale yellow mark on the gusset of her underpants most days and has been washing her in a bubble bath each night to help.

She started swimming lessons two months ago and often stays in her wet bathers afterwards. She passes urine without pain or urgency, her bowels open daily without straining, and she is her usual cheerful self at school.

data_table.Examination: Diffuse erythema of the vulval skin and the skin between the labia majora and the thighs, no vesicles, ulcers, fissures or excoriation, no bruising, hymen appears normal with no bleeding, scant non offensive discharge at the introitus, perianal skin intact and not excoriated, abdomen soft and non tender
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for leucocytes, nitrites and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days after sending a vulval swab for bacterial culture and sensitivities
options.rationale: Vulval swabs in prepubertal girls grow mixed perineal flora that do not guide treatment, and oral antibiotics do not alter the course of non specific vulvovaginitis. A swab is worth taking when there is offensive or purulent discharge, suggesting a specific pathogen such as group A streptococcus. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis

options.text: Prescribe topical clotrimazole cream twice daily for two weeks and review her symptoms at the end of that course
options.rationale: Candidal vulvovaginitis is rare before puberty because the unoestrogenised vagina has a neutral pH that does not favour candida, and it would be expected only after antibiotics, in nappy wearing children or with diabetes. Treating empirically with an antifungal delays the advice that actually works. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis

options.text: Give a single dose of mebendazole now and repeat it in two weeks, treating all members of the household together
options.rationale: Threadworm causes intense perianal itch that is worst at night and usually produces perianal excoriation, whereas this girl has vulval erythema with intact perianal skin and daytime symptoms. Mebendazole would be reasonable if the itch were nocturnal and perianal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Advise stopping bubble bath and soap, wearing loose cotton underwear, and applying a barrier ointment, then review
options.rationale: Non specific vulvovaginitis in prepubertal girls is an irritant dermatitis of thin unoestrogenised skin, and treatment is removal of the irritants together with a bland barrier preparation and attention to drying after swimming. Most improve within a few weeks on these measures alone, which is why review is planned rather than a prescription given. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis

options.text: Refer her for examination under anaesthesia and vaginoscopy to exclude a retained foreign body in the vagina
options.rationale: Vaginoscopy is indicated for persistent blood stained or foul discharge, which suggests a retained foreign body such as toilet paper, and for symptoms that do not respond to hygiene measures. A non offensive discharge with no bleeding does not justify an anaesthetic at this stage. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis

explanation.summary: Vulvovaginitis is the commonest gynaecological problem of prepubertal girls and in the large majority is non specific, driven by thin unoestrogenised vulval skin, close proximity of the anus, and contact irritants such as soap, bubble bath, shampoo and prolonged wet bathers. Symptoms are soreness, itch, dysuria at the vulva rather than within the urethra, and a scant discharge that marks the underwear. Management is education and irritant avoidance, with a barrier ointment to protect the skin and simple measures such as showering rather than bathing and drying thoroughly after swimming. Antibiotics, antifungals and swabs are not part of routine care, but specific causes are considered when the discharge is purulent or offensive, when there is bleeding, or when symptoms persist despite good hygiene. Persistent blood stained discharge warrants vaginoscopy for a foreign body, and any behavioural change, genital injury or specific disclosure requires assessment for sexual abuse.
key_points: Non specific vulvovaginitis is an irritant dermatitis, so the treatment is removal of irritants plus a barrier preparation.
Vulval swabs usually grow mixed flora and are reserved for offensive or purulent discharge.
Candida is rare before puberty because the vaginal pH is neutral without oestrogen.
Nocturnal perianal itch with excoriation points to threadworm rather than to vulvovaginitis.
Persistent bloody or foul discharge raises a retained foreign body and warrants vaginoscopy.
explanation.pearls: Dysuria in a prepubertal girl with a negative dipstick is usually urine stinging inflamed vulval skin rather than a urinary tract infection, and asking whether the pain is felt outside or inside distinguishes the two at the bedside.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on vulvovaginitis
BMJ Best Practice: Vulvovaginitis in children

subtopic_detail: Eight months of sound repetition with visible facial tension in a three year old whose language is otherwise typical
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a three year old boy whose parents are worried about his speech. For about eight months he has repeated the first sound of words, and in the last two months they have noticed his eyes screw up and his jaw tighten as he pushes a word out.

He has begun to say things such as it is too hard and to give up on sentences. He uses four to five word sentences, follows two step instructions, plays imaginatively with his older sister and passed his newborn hearing screen. His father stuttered as a child and did not receive treatment until he was ten.

data_table.Examination: Repetition of initial sounds on about one in five words with two audible blocks during the consultation, visible tension around the eyes and jaw during blocks, normal articulation between dysfluencies, vocabulary and sentence structure appropriate for age, responds to conversational speech at normal volume from across the room, oromotor examination normal with symmetrical palatal elevation and normal tongue movement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Reassure the parents that most preschool dysfluency resolves and arrange to review his speech in twelve months
options.rationale: Natural recovery is common in the first year of dysfluency, but this boy has already stuttered for eight months, has developed physical tension and negative reaction to his own speech, and has a first degree relative who stuttered, which are the features that predict persistence. Waiting another year forfeits the preschool window in which treatment works best. (Source: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on stuttering)
source_refs: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on stuttering

options.text: Advise the parents to ask him to slow down, take a breath and repeat the word each time he becomes stuck
options.rationale: Instructing a child to slow down or start again draws attention to the moment of stuttering and tends to increase struggle and avoidance rather than reduce dysfluency. Parents are instead coached within a structured program to give specific contingent feedback about smooth speech. (Source: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on stuttering)
source_refs: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on stuttering

options.text: Refer him to a paediatrician for a multidisciplinary autism assessment before considering any speech intervention
options.rationale: Autism assessment is prompted by differences in social communication, restricted interests or repetitive behaviour, whereas this boy converses, plays imaginatively and uses age appropriate sentence structure. Referring him down that pathway delays the intervention he needs. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on speech and language delay)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on speech and language delay

options.text: Arrange formal audiology assessment and defer any decision about speech therapy until the hearing result is known
options.rationale: Hearing loss produces articulation and language difficulties rather than repetition of initial sounds with physical struggle, and this boy responds to conversational speech across the room with age appropriate language. Audiology is a reasonable background check but is not the step that changes his outcome. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on speech and language delay)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on speech and language delay

options.text: Refer him now to a speech pathologist for assessment and a parent delivered early stuttering treatment program
options.rationale: Stuttering that has persisted beyond twelve months, or that carries risk markers such as physical tension, avoidance and a family history, warrants referral rather than further watchful waiting, and preschool treatment delivered by parents under speech pathology supervision has the strongest evidence for eliminating stuttering. Treatment is most effective before school entry, when the child's reaction to his own speech is still forming. (Source: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on stuttering)
source_refs: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on stuttering

explanation.summary: Stuttering typically begins between two and four years of age and affects up to eight per cent of preschool children, with natural recovery in many during the first year after onset. The decision that matters in primary care is whether to watch or to refer, and it turns on duration since onset, the presence of secondary features such as facial tension, blocks and avoidance, the child's own distress, and a family history of persistent stuttering. Early intervention delivered by parents under speech pathology supervision, of which the Lidcombe Program developed in Australia is the best studied example, produces high rates of resolution when started in the preschool years. Untreated persistent stuttering is associated with social anxiety and reduced educational and occupational participation in adolescence and adulthood, which is why the preschool window is defended. Advice that puts the child on the spot, such as telling him to slow down or start the word again, tends to worsen struggle behaviour.
key_points: Natural recovery is common in the first twelve months after onset, so duration since onset is a central triage question.
Physical tension, blocks, avoidance of words or speaking situations, and family history all predict persistence.
Parent delivered behavioural treatment supervised by a speech pathologist is the intervention with the strongest evidence in preschoolers.
Asking a child to slow down or repeat a word increases attention to the stutter and is not recommended.
Normal sentence structure, comprehension and social play separate stuttering from language disorder and from autism.
explanation.pearls: The strongest single trigger for referral rather than watchful waiting is dysfluency persisting beyond twelve months from onset, because natural recovery rates fall sharply after that point and treatment before school entry has substantially better outcomes than treatment in the school years.

sources.label: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on stuttering
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on speech and language delay
